lead: Electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) means that every electrical part of a vehicle works properly in the electrical noise made by the others, and does not make enough noise itself to upset them or nearby receivers. A car is a hard place for this: sparks of many kilovolts, sparking motor brushes and switched coils sit a few centimetres from ECUs that read millivolt sensor signals and radios that pick up microvolt broadcasts. Interference suppression keeps the noise down at its source, blocks its path and hardens the receiver.
prereq: You need: the 12 V supply and the circuit diagrams of Chapter 1.2, and the idea of inductance and capacitance from first-year physics.

blocks.text: Every EMC problem has three parts. The source makes the disturbance. The coupling path carries it. The sink (the victim) is the part that misbehaves. EMC has two sides: emission, how much noise a part sends out, and immunity (also called susceptibility), how much noise a part can take without a fault.

items: Sources inside the vehicle: the ignition spark (a very fast current pulse that radiates up to hundreds of megahertz); commutator motors, whose brushes spark; the alternator diodes; relays, solenoids and injectors, which give spikes when switched off; PWM drivers; and the load dump, a surge when the battery is disconnected while the alternator is charging.
Sources outside: broadcast and mobile-phone transmitters, radar, high-voltage power lines, and electrostatic discharge from a person's hand.
Sinks: the radio and other receivers (long, medium and FM bands, digital radio, GPS), ECU inputs and sensor lines, and the data buses that join the ECUs.

blocks.text: A disturbance on the supply line is called a transient. Switching off an inductive load can put a negative spike of a hundred volts or more on its wire. A load dump in a 12 V system, if it is not suppressed, can raise the bus to around a hundred volts for a few hundred milliseconds, enough to destroy electronics. International test standards describe these pulses so that every supplier tests against the same shapes: ISO 7637-2 for conducted transients, ISO 16750-2 for the load dump, CISPR 25 for radio emissions from components, and the ISO 11452 series for immunity to radiated fields.
There are four coupling paths, and the remedy depends on which one carries the noise.

items: Conducted (galvanic) coupling: two circuits share a wire or ground point. Current from a noisy load flows through the shared resistance and the voltage drop appears in the quiet circuit. A long common ground return is the usual culprit.

Capacitive coupling: two wires run side by side, and a fast voltage change on one pushes current into the other through the small capacitance between them. It grows with dv/dt, the rate of change of voltage.
Inductive coupling: a changing current makes a changing magnetic field, which induces a voltage in any nearby loop. It grows with di/dt and with the loop area.
Radiated coupling: at high frequency a wire acts as an aerial. A harness wire about a quarter of a wavelength long (75 cm at 100 MHz) radiates and receives well.

blocks.where: X<sub>C</sub> and X<sub>L</sub> are the reactances of a capacitor and an inductor in ohms (Ω); f is the frequency in hertz (Hz); C is capacitance in farads (F); L is inductance in henries (H). A capacitor is a low impedance to high-frequency noise and an inductor (choke) is a high impedance, which is why both are used to keep noise off the supply.

blocks.text: Suppression works best at the source, then on the path, last at the sink.

items: At the source: a freewheeling diode, an RC network or a varistor across every relay and solenoid coil; capacitors across DC motor brushes and at the alternator B+ terminal; chokes in motor supply lines; resistor spark plugs and suppression resistors in plug caps or HT leads, which slow the spark current pulse; and Zener power diodes in the alternator rectifier, which clamp the load-dump surge.

On the path: keep wires short; route power wires away from signal wires; use twisted pairs (the CAN bus) so that induced voltages cancel; use screened cables for aerials and sensitive sensors; bond the engine, body and exhaust together with short, wide ground straps; and bring sensor grounds to one clean point instead of the nearest bolt.
At the sink: filter capacitors and ferrites on ECU inputs, metal housings, software that ignores implausible values.

blocks.text: A vehicle is tested twice: each component on a bench to CISPR 25 limits, and the whole vehicle in a screened, absorber-lined room.

examples.question: A 12 V relay coil has a resistance of 85 Ω and an inductance of 0.20 H. It is switched off by a transistor in the ECU. (a) Find the coil current and the energy stored in the coil. (b) Without suppression, the transistor would try to stop this current in 2 µs. Estimate the voltage the coil would try to produce. (c) A freewheeling diode (0.7 V drop) is fitted across the coil. Find the time constant of the current decay and the time for the current to fall to 10 % of its value.
steps: Coil current: I = V ÷ R = 12 V ÷ 85 Ω = 0.141 A.
Stored energy: W = ½ L I² = 0.5 × 0.20 H × (0.141 A)² = 1.99 × 10⁻³ J ≈ 2.0 mJ.

Induced voltage if the current stops in 2 µs: V = L × di/dt = 0.20 H × 0.141 A ÷ (2 × 10⁻⁶ s) = 14,100 V. In practice the transistor breaks down long before, or an arc forms, and that spike is the interference.
With the diode, the coil current keeps flowing round the loop through the diode, so the coil voltage is clamped at about 0.7 V and the transistor sees only 12 V + 0.7 V = 12.7 V.
The current then decays through the coil's own resistance with time constant τ = L ÷ R = 0.20 H ÷ 85 Ω = 2.35 ms.
Time to fall to 10 %: t = τ × ln 10 = 2.35 ms × 2.303 = 5.4 ms.
examples.answer: The coil carries 0.141 A and stores about 2.0 mJ; unsuppressed it would try to make about 14 kV, but with the diode the transistor sees only 12.7 V and the current dies away with τ = 2.35 ms, reaching 10 % after about 5.4 ms (so the relay releases a few milliseconds later than without the diode).

examples.question: A radiator fan motor is suppressed with an LC low-pass filter in its supply: a 5 µH choke in series and a 1 µF capacitor to ground. (a) Find the cut-off frequency. (b) Find the reactance of the choke and the capacitor at 1 MHz, in the medium-wave radio band. (c) An ideal two-element LC filter falls by 40 dB per decade above cut-off. Estimate the attenuation at 1 MHz.
steps: Choke at 1 MHz: X<sub>L</sub> = 2πfL = 2π × 10⁶ × 5 × 10⁻⁶ = 31.4 Ω, a high series impedance for the noise.
Capacitor at 1 MHz: X<sub>C</sub> = 1 ÷ (2πfC) = 1 ÷ (2π × 10⁶ × 10⁻⁶) = 0.159 Ω, a near short to ground for the noise.
Decades above cut-off: log₁₀(1 MHz ÷ 71.2 kHz) = log₁₀(14.05) = 1.148.
Attenuation ≈ 40 dB × 1.148 = 45.9 dB, so the noise voltage is cut to about 1/200 of its value (10^(45.9/20) = 197).
The motor's own 12 V DC supply passes untouched, because at 0 Hz the choke is a short wire and the capacitor is an open circuit.
examples.answer: The cut-off is 71.2 kHz; at 1 MHz the choke is 31.4 Ω and the capacitor 0.159 Ω, and the filter cuts the noise by about 46 dB (about 200 times) while letting the DC through.

traps: EMC is two-sided: low emission and enough immunity. Answers that only describe suppression of the ignition miss half the topic.
A freewheeling diode must be fitted with its cathode to the positive end of the coil. Fitted the other way, it shorts the supply when the relay is switched on.
A freewheeling diode slows the release of a relay. Where fast release matters, a Zener or resistor is added in series with the diode.
Capacitive coupling grows with dv/dt and inductive coupling with di/dt; mixing them up gives the wrong remedy (screening against electric fields, twisting and small loops against magnetic fields).
Resistor spark plugs and suppression leads reduce radio interference, not spark energy needed for ignition; replacing them with plain plugs is a common cause of radio noise.

quiz.q: Define electromagnetic compatibility and name its two sides.
quiz.a: EMC is the ability of a device to work properly in its electromagnetic surroundings without disturbing other devices. Its two sides are emission and immunity (susceptibility).

quiz.q: Explain why CAN bus wires are twisted together.
quiz.a: A changing magnetic field induces voltages in each small loop of the pair, but the twist reverses the loop direction every half turn, so the induced voltages cancel. Noise that reaches both wires equally is also rejected because CAN reads the difference between the wires.

quiz.q: What is a load dump and how is it limited in a 12 V system?
quiz.a: It is a voltage surge when the battery is disconnected while the alternator is charging: the alternator's field cannot collapse at once, so the bus can rise to around a hundred volts for a few hundred milliseconds. Zener power diodes in the rectifier or a central suppressor clamp it.

quiz.q: A 0.47 µF suppression capacitor sits at the alternator B+ terminal. Find its reactance at 100 Hz (ripple region) and at 1 MHz.
quiz.a: X<sub>C</sub> = 1 ÷ (2πfC). At 100 Hz: 1 ÷ (2π × 100 × 0.47 × 10⁻⁶) = 3386 Ω. At 1 MHz: 1 ÷ (2π × 10⁶ × 0.47 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.339 Ω, so it shorts radio-frequency noise to ground but barely loads the bus.

quiz.q: A radio crackles only when the engine runs, and the crackle rises with engine speed. Analyse the likely source and path and give two checks.
quiz.a: Noise that tracks engine speed comes from the ignition (crackle) or the alternator (whine). Check that resistor plugs and suppression caps or leads are fitted and that the engine-to-body ground strap is tight and clean; then check the alternator suppression capacitor and the aerial screen ground. A missing ground strap turns the whole engine into a noise source on the body.

beyond: Not for the exam. Electric vehicles make EMC harder: traction inverters switch hundreds of amperes at hundreds of volts in tens of nanoseconds, so screened high-voltage cables and filters are standard. Search for CISPR 25 test set-up and ISO 7637 pulses.
